106.title: Lord, have mercy
106.hook: three short Greek cries left inside the Latin Mass
106.howItsDone: Near the start of Mass, after the penitential act (or as part of it), the Kyrie is said or sung, usually twice for each line: Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy, in English or in the original Greek.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Confiteor: through my fault, and a fist on the chest. Your line was we all begin as sinners. Did you catch yourself feeling above someone? Day one hundred and six.

For about fifteen hundred years, the Mass in the West was said in Latin. Every word of it. The readings, the prayers, the priest's words over the bread. Latin, Latin, Latin. Except for one moment near the start. Right after the confession you heard about yesterday, the choir or the people would sing three short cries in a completely different language. Not Latin. Greek. It's like finding one line of an old family song, in grandma's language, still sung in the middle of a house where nobody speaks it anymore. Nobody translated it out. Today, those three cries.
screen: `FIFTEEN HUNDRED YEARS OF LATIN.` → `ONE MOMENT IN GREEK.` → `NOBODY TRANSLATED IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Kyrie eleison. Lord, have mercy. Christe eleison. Christ, have mercy. Kyrie eleison. Lord, have mercy. Kyrios is Greek for Lord, the word the first Christians used for Jesus. Eleison means have mercy. The cry came into the Roman Mass from the Greek-speaking churches of the East, and when the West prayed in Latin, this piece was kept in its original tongue, like a stitch that holds the two halves of the Church together. For centuries each cry was repeated three times, nine in all. Now it's usually twice each, six in all, and often said or sung in English. Now listen to where this cry comes from. It isn't a church invention. It's the cry of desperate people on the road in the Gospels. Two blind men sitting by the road hear Jesus passing, and shout: have mercy on us. A mother from outside Israel, whose daughter is suffering, follows him shouting, in the Douay-Rheims: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou son of David." People who had run out of every other option. So the Kyrie at Mass is the whole church standing in the place of those people on the roadside. Here's one more thing hiding in the word. The Greek for mercy, eleos, gave a word for giving to the poor, eleēmosynē. That word traveled through Latin into Old English and shrank, over centuries, into our word alms. Mercy that you ask for, and mercy that you give, come from the same root.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mercy, three times. Settle, and breathe. Breathe in slowly. On the out-breath, if you pray, say quietly: Kyrie eleison. Breathe in. Christe eleison. Breathe in. Kyrie eleison. If you don't pray, you can simply let three slow breaths go, thinking of someone, maybe yourself, who could use mercy today. Then let the quiet stay. The bell holds the time.
Kyrie eleison. Greek for Lord, have mercy: the cry of the roadside, kept in Greek inside the Latin Mass. Today's word.
Your line: mercy, three times. Today, give one small mercy of your own: some alms, a let-it-go, a second chance. Day one hundred and six.

107.title: The Gloria (Luke 2:14)
107.hook: the angels' song from Bethlehem, silent in Advent and Lent
107.carry: glory to god in the highest
107.howItsDone: The Gloria is sung or said after the Kyrie at Sunday Masses outside Advent and Lent, and on solemnities and feasts; on Holy Thursday and at the Easter Vigil the church bells ring during it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kyrie eleison, Lord, have mercy, kept in Greek. Your line was mercy, three times. What small mercy did you give? Day one hundred and seven.

Go back eighty days, to the shepherds. A night on the hills outside Bethlehem. Sheep, cold, a fire, nothing happening. Then an angel, and a light, and terror, and the news: a child is born. And then, Luke says, suddenly there's a whole crowd of angels, a heavenly army, and they're praising God. It's the first Christmas song, and it's one line long. Every Sunday, right after the church has asked for mercy, it picks up that song and keeps going with it. For four weeks before Christmas and six weeks before Easter, it goes quiet. And when it comes back, the bells ring. Today: the Gloria.
screen: `THE SHEPHERDS' HILLSIDE.` → `A CROWD OF ANGELS.` → `THE FIRST CHRISTMAS SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the angels' line, in the Douay-Rheims: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." In Latin, Gloria in excelsis Deo. That's the start of the hymn. But the Gloria at Mass goes much further than the angels did. Christians in the first few centuries kept singing after that line, adding praise upon praise. In Latin: laudamus te, benedicimus te, adoramus te, glorificamus te. Praise, blessing, adoring, glorifying, one after another. Then it turns to Jesus as the Lamb of God, who takes away the world's sins, and asks his mercy. And it ends with the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, like the Glory Be you learned, but bigger. That's why it's sometimes called the greater doxology. The Glory Be is the little glory-word. This is the big one. Notice where it sits. Right after the church asks for mercy, it bursts into praise. Sorry, then glory. The mood flips. And here's the part that makes it powerful: it isn't sung every week. In Advent, the weeks before Christmas, it's left out, so the angels' song can come back new on Christmas night. In Lent, it's silent too. On Holy Thursday, it's sung while every bell in the church rings, and then the bells go silent until Easter. At the Easter Vigil, the Gloria returns, and the bells ring again. One small scholar's note: the King James Bible reads good will toward men. The Latin tradition reads peace to men of good will. The difference is one letter in some Greek manuscripts.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one line of praise. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say or hum one line: glory to God in the highest. Quietly is fine. Tunelessly is fine. The shepherds weren't choir material either. If you don't pray, find one thing today that's simply good, and say so out loud: that's beautiful. Something that asks for nothing back. Then sit with it. The bell holds the time.

108.title: The readings and the psalm
108.hook: Sundays run a three-year cycle so most of the Bible is read aloud
108.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass, lay readers usually proclaim the first and second readings from the ambo, a cantor leads the responsorial psalm, and the readings follow a three-year cycle (Years A, B and C) shared by Catholic parishes worldwide.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gloria, the angels' song, silent in Advent and Lent. Your line was glory to God in the highest. What good thing did you praise? Day one hundred and eight.

The Gloria ends, and everyone sits down. That's the signal. The first part of the Mass, the gathering and the mercy and the praise, is over. Now comes the second: listening. A person walks up to a stand called the ambo. Very often it isn't the priest. It's a parishioner, a teacher or a retired mailman or a nervous sixteen-year-old, reading from a big book to a room full of people. And the passage they read wasn't chosen by the priest that week, or by them. It was chosen decades ago, for this exact Sunday, by a plan that runs across three years. Today's word is the name of that book.
screen: `EVERYONE SITS.` → `A PARISHIONER AT THE AMBO.` → `CHOSEN DECADES AGO.`

segments.voice: Lectionary comes from the Latin lectio, a reading. It's the book of readings for Mass, laid out day by day. After the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s, the bishops asked for the treasures of the Bible to be opened up much more richly to the people. So a new lectionary was built, and it came into use in 1970. Here's how it works on a Sunday. There are four readings. First, usually from the Old Testament, chosen to echo the Gospel of the day. Then a psalm, sung or said: a cantor sings the verses, and everyone answers with a short refrain. Then a reading from one of the letters of the apostles, often Paul. Then the Gospel. And the Sundays run in a three-year cycle. Year A reads mostly from Matthew. Year B, Mark. Year C, Luke. John comes in around the great seasons, Lent and Easter, and fills out the short year of Mark. So over three years of Sundays, a Catholic who comes every week hears a large share of the Bible read aloud. Not every word, but far more than before the reform, when one year of readings repeated over and over. Weekdays have their own two-year cycle. And here's the lovely part: on any given Sunday, Catholic churches around the world, in hundreds of languages, are reading the same passages. At the end of each reading, the reader says, in the old Latin, Verbum Domini, the word of the Lord. And the people answer, Deo gratias, thanks be to God.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear one line. Settle, and breathe. Here's a line from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." Let it sit. Say it again in your head, slower. Notice which word catches. Lamp. Feet. Paths. You don't have to decide what it means. Just carry it for a minute. If you pray, you can let it become your prayer. The bell holds the time.

109.title: The gospel
109.hook: everyone stands, three small crosses on forehead, lips and heart
109.howItsDone: At Mass the congregation stands for the Gospel, sings the Alleluia (another acclamation in Lent), and traces small crosses on forehead, lips and heart as the deacon or priest announces the reading; he kisses the book at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the readings and the psalm, laid out in the lectionary. Your line was the whole book, in turns. Did you look up Sunday's readings? Day one hundred and nine.

For the first readings, everyone sits. The psalm, still sitting. Then something changes. The whole church stands up, all at once, and starts to sing one word over and over: Alleluia. Candles move. Sometimes incense rises. A deacon or the priest lifts a big, often gold-covered book from the altar and carries it high to the ambo, like a banner. And when he announces which Gospel he's reading from, hundreds of people do something small and quick with their thumbs that visitors almost never catch. Forehead. Lips. Heart. Today: the Gospel.
screen: `EVERYONE STANDS.` → `ALLELUIA, AND THE BOOK HELD HIGH.` → `THREE SMALL CROSSES.`

segments.voice: Gospel is an old English word: god spel, good news. It translates the Greek euangelion, a word used in the Roman world for a herald's announcement, like news of a victory. Mark's Gospel opens with it, in the Douay-Rheims: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." For Catholics, the Gospel reading is the high point of the listening part of the Mass, because here Christ himself speaks, in his own words and deeds. So the body changes. Everyone stands, the way you'd stand when someone important walks in. Alleluia, a Hebrew word meaning praise the Lord, is sung to greet it. In Lent, when the Alleluia goes quiet, another short acclamation takes its place. Only a deacon or a priest reads the Gospel, and before he does, he quietly asks to be made worthy of it. Then he announces it: a reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew, or Mark, or Luke, or John. And that's when the thumbs move. A small cross on the forehead. A small cross on the lips. A small cross over the heart. Catholics often explain it as a silent prayer without words: may this word be in my mind, on my lips, and in my heart. Understand it, say it, love it. When the reading ends, the priest or deacon kisses the page. In Latin, he quietly says a line asking that through the words of the Gospel, our sins may be wiped away. A book, kissed. News worth standing up for.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three crosses, then a line. Settle, and breathe. If you're Catholic, or you'd like to try it, trace a small cross with your thumb on your forehead: in my mind. On your lips: on my lips. Over your heart: in my heart. If you'd rather not, just touch each place lightly, or simply notice it. Then bring back one line of a Gospel you know, any line, and let it sit in all three places. The bell holds the time.
The Gospel. Good news: the reading at Mass where Christ speaks, greeted by standing, Alleluia, and three small crosses. Today's word.
Your line: mind, lips, heart. Today, before you read anything that matters to you, trace those three crosses, or just pause at all three. Day one hundred and nine.

110.title: The homily
110.hook: the priest or deacon opens the readings for this crowd on this day
110.tomorrow: The Creed and the prayers of the faithful
110.howItsDone: After the Gospel, the congregation sits and the priest or deacon preaches the homily, drawn from the day's readings; it is required at Sunday and holy day Masses, and a short silence often follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gospel, good news, greeted with three small crosses. Your line was mind, lips, heart. Did you pause at all three before reading? Day one hundred and ten.

The Gospel ends. The book is kissed. Everyone sits down, and there's a small rustle as a few hundred people get comfortable, because they know what's next. The priest or deacon is going to talk. Everyone has a story about this part. The one who went on for forty minutes. The one who told the same joke every Easter. And the one, maybe once, who said something that landed so exactly on your week that you wondered if somebody had told him. Today's word is the name for what happens after the Gospel, and it's older and more interesting than a speech.
screen: `THE BOOK IS KISSED.` → `EVERYONE SITS.` → `THE ONE THAT LANDED.`

segments.voice: Homily comes from the Greek homilia, which means a conversation, a talk among people gathered together. Not a lecture from above. A conversation. The verb shows up in one of the stories you heard earlier on this path. On the road to Emmaus, two disciples are walking home, talking together about everything that has happened, and in Luke's Greek, the word for their talking is the same root. Then a stranger joins them and opens the scriptures to them. Later they say, in the Douay-Rheims: "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way, and opened to us the scriptures?" That's what a homily is meant to do. Take the readings everyone just heard and open them, for these people, on this day. Jesus did something like it in his hometown synagogue in Nazareth. He stood, read a passage from Isaiah, sat down, and with every eye on him said: "This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears." Not a history lesson. Today. So a homily isn't the same as a sermon on any topic. The Church asks that it grow out of the readings and the Mass itself. It's given by a priest or deacon, and it's required on Sundays and holy days. Pope Francis wrote pages on homilies, and asked that they be short, warm, and more like a mother talking to her children than a lecture. Afterward, the Church suggests a short silence, so what was said can settle. The word has been read. Now it's handed to you, for this week.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one sentence to keep. Settle, and breathe. Think of the best thing anyone ever said to you about life, from a pulpit, a classroom, a kitchen table, a friend at 2am. Just one sentence. If nothing comes, take the one from Nazareth: this day is fulfilled. Say it in your head. Then ask: what would it mean for today, this ordinary Tuesday or whatever day it is? If you pray, you can ask for ears to hear. The bell holds the time.
Homily. From the Greek for conversation: the priest or deacon opening the day's readings for the people in front of him. Today's word.
Your line: the word, for today. Today, write down one sentence you'd keep, from a sermon, a book, or a friend, somewhere you'll see it tonight. Day one hundred and ten.

111.title: The Creed and the prayers of the faithful
111.hook: the whole church says what it believes, then prays for the world
111.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass the congregation stands after the homily to profess the Nicene Creed, bowing at the words about the incarnation; then a deacon or reader announces the universal prayer, or prayers of the faithful, and the people respond to each intention.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the homily, a conversation that opens the readings. Your line was the word, for today. Which sentence did you keep? Day one hundred and eleven.

The year is 325, in a lakeside town called Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. About three hundred bishops have traveled there, some of them with scars from the persecutions only a few years before. One bishop is missing an eye. Another has crippled hands. The emperor himself has called the meeting, because the Church is tearing itself apart over one question: is Jesus fully God, or is he the first and greatest thing God made? What they decided that summer is still said out loud, every Sunday, by Catholics around the world and many other Christians too. Today: the Nicene Creed.

A priest in Alexandria named Arius had been teaching that the Son was created by the Father, glorious, but made. His followers even sang it: there was a time when he was not. The council said no. To pin it down, they reached for a Greek word: homoousios, of the same substance, the same being as the Father. In today's English Mass the word is consubstantial. Not a lesser god. Not a creature. God from God, light from light. A second council, at Constantinople in 381, added more about the Holy Spirit, and that longer creed is the one said at Mass today, right after the homily. You learned the shorter Apostles' Creed ten days ago. This one is its bigger sibling, built for an argument. One honest detail. Centuries later, churches in the West added a phrase saying the Spirit comes from the Father and the Son. In Latin, filioque. Orthodox Christians never accepted that addition, and it remains one of the questions between the churches. Many Eastern Catholics say the creed without it. Then, straight after the creed, the Mass turns outward. The prayers of the faithful. Someone reads short intentions: for the Church, for leaders of nations, for people who are suffering, for the sick and the dead of this parish. After each, everyone answers together, asking God to hear. Paul asked for this, in the Douay-Rheims: "that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men." First the church says what it believes. Then, believing it, the church asks.

Your line: we believe, then we ask. Today, when you hear about someone in trouble, don't just scroll past. Stop, and ask on their behalf, in whatever way is yours. Day one hundred and eleven.

112.title: The gifts come up
112.hook: bread and wine are carried forward; a drop of water mingles with the wine
112.howItsDone: At the preparation of the gifts, a collection is taken, members of the congregation often carry the bread and wine to the altar, the priest blesses God over each, adds a drop of water to the wine, and washes his hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nicene Creed and the prayers of the faithful. Your line was we believe, then we ask. Whose trouble did you stop for? Day one hundred and twelve.

The prayers for the world end, and the whole feel of the Mass shifts. People sit. Baskets start moving down the rows, and there's the rustle of envelopes and a kid proudly dropping in a coin. Up front, servers are laying a white cloth on the altar, setting down a cup and a book. And then, from the back of the church, a few ordinary people walk up the aisle. A couple, maybe, or a family with a nervous child. They're carrying a plate of bread and a small glass jug of wine. They hand them to the priest and go back to their seats. It looks like nothing. Today: the offertory.
screen: `BASKETS DOWN THE ROWS.` → `A FAMILY WALKS UP THE AISLE.` → `BREAD AND WINE, HANDED OVER.`

segments.voice: Offertory comes from the Latin offerre, to bring forward, to offer. The Mass has two great halves. The first is the word: readings, homily, creed, prayers. The second, starting now, is the Eucharist, the meal. And it starts with ordinary people carrying up ordinary things. Bread, which the earth gave and human hands made. Wine, the same. In the early Church, people often brought bread and wine from their own homes, and the leftovers went to the poor. The collection is the same idea: the people's gifts, for the Church and the poor, carried up with the bread. Then the priest lifts the bread a little and blesses God for it, in a prayer shaped like something much older. It echoes the Jewish blessings said over bread and wine at the table, the ones that begin baruch atah, blessed are you, the kind Jesus himself would have said. Now watch the wine. The priest or deacon pours it into the chalice, and then adds a single drop of water. Just a drop. He says a short prayer under his breath, borrowed from an ancient Christmas prayer: it asks that, since Christ came to share our humanity, we might come to share his divinity. The water disappears into the wine. It can't be taken back out. Catholics see in it the human joined to the divine, and some see the water and blood from Christ's side on the cross. Then the priest washes his hands. Looking back over this week, from mercy and glory to the readings, the Gospel, the homily and the creed: the word has been given. Now the ordinary things go up.
screen: `OFFERRE: TO BRING FORWARD.` · `ORDINARY PEOPLE, ORDINARY BREAD.` · `A BLESSING OLDER THAN THE MASS.` · `ONE DROP OF WATER IN THE WINE.` · then: `THE ORDINARY, CARRIED UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry up one small thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of one ordinary piece of your day. The commute. A sink of dishes. A spreadsheet. The kids' bedtime. Nothing impressive. Now picture carrying it forward in your hands, like that family in the aisle, and setting it down. If you pray, you can offer it to God, like a drop in the wine. If you don't, simply let it count, as part of something larger. The bell holds the time.
Offertory. The bringing forward of bread and wine, and the people's gifts, at the start of the Eucharist. Today's word.
Your line: the ordinary is carried up. Today, pick one dull task and do it as if you were carrying it up the aisle. Day one hundred and twelve.
